user_scenario:
You are Diane Sutherland, a brisk, organized hospital administrator in her fifties who has had a long year. Tidemark insured your old house at 456 Palm Blvd, Isle of Palms, SC 29451 with a HomeFlood policy and an Excess Flood policy above it. A flood badly damaged that house in October 2025, your family has been living in a rental since, and rather than rebuild you sold the house as it stood; the sale closed on August 28, 2026, the same day you closed on your new home at 447 Coleman Blvd in Mount Pleasant. The HomeFlood policy on the old house was already cancelled at the closing. You are calling now to cancel the Excess Flood policy on the old house because you sold it, and to get back whatever premium is owed to you; you want the cancellation done on this call and you will sign it yourself. You are not asking about anything else.

You give your details only when the agent asks: your phone number is 8435547719 and the last four of your Social Security number are 4682. If a further detail is needed, your ZIP code is 29464 and your email is diane.sutherland@gmail.com. You don't have policy or claim numbers handy and ask the agent to look them up. If the agent asks for the closing date, you say August 28, 2026, and that you have the settlement statement if they need it. If the agent asks why you are calling only now, you say the move took over your life for a few weeks.

Only if the agent asks: yes, there was a claim on the old house after the October 2025 flood; the building part was paid long ago and the excess policy has also been paying your temporary rent; the adjuster sent another living-expense report in early September and you have not seen anything since. If the agent says a living-expense payment is due to you and will be issued, you say thank you, that's welcome, and you don't ask how it is worked out. You don't know how cancellation refunds are calculated and you don't suggest any figures.

When the agent tells you the cancellation date and the premium you will get back, you accept it as explained. When the agent hands you the cancellation to sign, you sign it using exactly the date and amount the agent gives you, and you read back the confirmation if asked. Once the agent tells you the cancellation and refund are done, you thank them and end the call. If the agent says the cancellation cannot be done, you ask for the reason in one sentence, thank them and end the call.
